error_modes.label: Takeoff airspeed on the interval takeoff

texts.0: SP, due to a rotation input made off the runway picture while attention stayed on the departing lead, did not execute the takeoff with the standard airspeed. The aircraft was rotated below the computed rotation speed, where the criterion allows no tolerance at all on the low side, and the airspeed then overshot the standard by more than 10 knots as the aircraft accelerated in the climb. IP intervened on the controls to set the takeoff attitude and to bring the airspeed back to the standard value.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan that remained outside on lead instead of alternating to the airspeed indication during the ground roll, did not execute the takeoff with the standard airspeed. The airspeed stabilized about 10 knots above standard, at the outer limit of the one-sided tolerance, and SP reduced the excess only after two verbal prompts from IP. The fast condition was carried unchanged into the initial climb behind lead.
texts.2: SP, due to power and pitch handling aimed at closing the interval rather than at the published takeoff speed, allowed the takeoff airspeed to build past the standard. The excess reached roughly 7 knots, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, and SP identified it on the indicator and reset the takeoff attitude without prompting. No IP control input was required at any point of the takeoff.
texts.3: SP executed the interval takeoff with the standard airspeed, rotating at the computed speed with no deviation on the low side and holding the excess inside 5 knots. The scan alternated between the runway, lead and the airspeed indication, and pitch corrections were small and applied immediately.
texts.4: SP rotated exactly at the computed takeoff speed and held the standard airspeed through lift-off and the initial climb, with deviations that were negligible against the published tolerance. The presence of lead ahead produced no distortion of the speed schedule, and the airspeed never trended toward the low side where no tolerance exists.
texts.marginal: SP kept the takeoff airspeed inside standards but consistently on the fast side, with the excess sitting in the upper part of the acceptable band on each interval takeoff of the sortie. The trend came from accelerating early to reduce the spacing on lead rather than from control technique, and it repeated without further degradation. SP is expected to fly the published takeoff speed first and to manage the interval after the aircraft is clean and climbing.

texts_at.0: SP flew the interval takeoff with the scan between lead and the airspeed indication talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first interval takeoff at this stage and alternating the scan to the airspeed indication during the roll has not yet formed. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to alternate the scan to the airspeed indication during the roll without the reminder on the next interval takeoffs.
texts_at.1: SP stabilized the takeoff airspeed about 10 knots above standard, at the tolerance limit, because the scan stayed outside on lead through most of the ground roll before IP prompted the airspeed indication twice. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to alternate the scan to the airspeed indication during the roll rather than waiting for it to be prompted.
texts_at.2: SP let the takeoff airspeed build to roughly 7 knots above standard, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the handling was aimed at closing the interval rather than at the published speed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to fly the published takeoff speed first and manage the interval once the aircraft is climbing.
texts_at.3: SP held the takeoff airspeed inside 5 knots of standard on three of the four interval takeoffs, the fourth needing a small correction after a scan that favored lead a moment too long. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold that same scan balance on every takeoff that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP stabilized the takeoff airspeed to about 10 knots above standard, at the tolerance limit, once the scan was brought back to the airspeed indication. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP let the takeoff airspeed build toward 7 knots above standard while closing the interval but identified it on the indicator and reset the takeoff attitude without prompting, with no IP control input required. Flying the published takeoff speed first, rather than closing the interval before it is set, would trim that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good takeoff airspeed control on the interval departure.
texts_above.3: SP executed the interval takeoff with the standard airspeed, rotating at the computed speed with no deviation on the low side and holding the excess inside 5 knots, the scan alternating between the runway, lead and the airspeed indication. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good takeoff airspeed control on the interval departure.
texts_above.4: SP rotated exactly at the computed takeoff speed and held the standard airspeed through lift-off and the initial climb, with the presence of lead ahead producing no distortion of the speed schedule. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent takeoff airspeed control on the interval departure.

error_modes.label: Runway centerline tracking during the interval takeoff roll
error_modes.source: specific:Maintain in the center line of RWY (ft)

texts.0: SP, due to rudder input insufficient for the yaw produced at power application and for the reported crosswind, did not maintain the A/C at the centerline during the takeoff roll. Lateral displacement passed 10 feet and continued to diverge toward the runway edge as the aircraft accelerated behind lead. IP took the controls to re-establish the takeoff track before rotation.
texts.1: SP, due to directional corrections applied in discrete steps while attention was divided between the runway and lead ahead, did not maintain the A/C at the centerline during the takeoff roll. Displacement reached about 10 feet, at the limit of the allowed deviation, and SP re-centered the aircraft only after IP called for rudder. The aircraft lifted off with the track still offset from the assigned side of the runway.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow initial response to the swing at power application, drifted off the runway centerline by roughly 8 feet during the interval takeoff. The deviation stayed between the code 3 and code 1 limits and SP corrected it with coordinated rudder well before rotation, with no prompting and no IP action. The takeoff track was then held for the rest of the ground roll.
texts.3: SP maintained the A/C at the centerline during the interval takeoff with lateral deviation held inside 5 feet. Rudder inputs were continuous and matched to the yaw from power application and to the crosswind, and the same track was carried through rotation and lift-off.
texts.4: SP held the aircraft on the runway centerline with deviations barely perceptible against the runway markings, from brake release to lift-off. Directional inputs anticipated the yaw rather than reacting to it, and the takeoff track was preserved unchanged into the initial climb behind lead.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft inside the centerline tolerance but with a persistent offset toward lead that was held rather than removed for most of the ground roll. The offset stayed within standards and did not grow, but it reduced the lateral margin available if lead had aborted. SP is expected to re-center the aircraft as soon as the offset is detected instead of tracking parallel to the centerline.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the centerline on the interval takeoff with the rudder correction for the swing talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first interval takeoff at this stage and dividing the scan between lead and the runway without letting the centerline correction wait has not yet formed. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to divide the scan between lead and the runway without letting the centerline correction wait for a call without the reminder on the next interval takeoffs.
texts_at.1: SP re-centered the aircraft only after IP called for rudder, with the takeoff track displaced to about 10 feet, at the tolerance limit, because attention was divided between the runway and lead ahead. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to divide the scan between lead and the runway without letting the centerline correction wait for a call.
texts_at.2: SP drifted off the centerline by roughly 8 feet, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the initial response to the swing at power application was slow. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to respond to the swing at power application as promptly as the correction that followed it.
texts_at.3: SP held the centerline inside 5 feet through rotation and lift-off on three of the four interval takeoffs, the fourth needing a small correction after a rudder input applied a beat late. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold that same track on every takeoff that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP re-centered the aircraft, holding the takeoff track displaced to about 10 feet, at the tolerance limit, before the correction was completed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP drifted off the centerline by roughly 8 feet during the interval takeoff but corrected it with coordinated rudder well before rotation, with no prompting and no IP action. Responding to the swing at power application as promptly as the correction that followed, rather than after the drift builds, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound centerline discipline on the interval roll.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the aircraft at the centerline during the interval takeoff with lateral deviation held inside 5 feet, rudder inputs continuous and matched to the yaw from power application and the wind alike. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed centerline discipline on the interval roll.
texts_above.4: SP held the aircraft on the runway centerline with deviations barely perceptible against the runway markings from brake release to lift-off, anticipating the yaw instead of reacting to it. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional centerline discipline on the interval roll.

error_modes.label: Brake release timing and takeoff interval behind lead

texts.0: SP, due to brake release made on the sight of lead moving rather than on the briefed timing reference, did not establish the briefed takeoff interval. The spacing at lift-off was less than half the briefed interval and the aircraft was closing on lead inside the wake region while still accelerating. IP intervened with power and lateral displacement to open the spacing to a safe value.
texts.1: SP, due to a start of the timing count taken at the wrong point of lead's roll, did not establish the briefed takeoff interval. The spacing at brake release was short of the briefed value by a margin that placed the aircraft at the limit of the acceptable band, and SP opened it only after IP directed a power reduction. The correction was made late, with the aircraft already airborne.
texts.2: SP, due to a hesitation in advancing the power after the timing count was complete, released brakes later than the briefed interval required. The spacing opened beyond the briefed value but stayed inside the band that still allows a normal rejoin, and SP recognized the excess and closed it with a controlled power setting on SP's own initiative. No prompting and no IP input were needed.
texts.3: SP released brakes at the briefed interval behind lead, timed from the correct reference point of lead's takeoff roll. The spacing at lift-off matched the briefed value and required no power change beyond the normal takeoff setting to maintain it.
texts.4: SP established the briefed takeoff interval exactly, with brake release timed to the second and power applied in one continuous movement. The spacing was held constant through lift-off and gear retraction, so that the rejoin geometry was set up without any corrective action.
texts.marginal: SP established the briefed takeoff interval within acceptable limits, but consistently at the short end of the band on every interval takeoff of the sortie. The spacing remained legal and no closure problem developed, yet it left little margin for a slow acceleration by lead. SP is expected to time brake release so that the interval is centered on the briefed value rather than set at its minimum.

texts_at.0: SP timed brake release for the interval takeoff with the count from lead's roll talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first interval takeoff at this stage and timing the count from the correct point of lead's roll has not yet formed. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to time the count from the correct point of lead's roll without the reminder on the next interval takeoffs.
texts_at.1: SP opened the interval only after IP directed a power reduction, having released brakes with the spacing short of the briefed value by a margin at the limit of the acceptable band. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to time the count from the correct point of lead's roll rather than needing the spacing opened by direction.
texts_at.2: SP released brakes later than the briefed interval required, opening the spacing beyond the briefed value but inside the band that still allows a normal rejoin, then closed it with a controlled power setting without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the timing count from the correct reference point rather than adjusting the excess afterward.
texts_at.3: SP released brakes at the briefed interval behind lead on three of the four takeoffs, the fourth spacing needing a small power correction after a count started a beat off the correct reference. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to start that one count as precisely as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP opened the interval, with the spacing corrected from short of the briefed value once the power reduction was applied. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP released brakes later than the briefed interval required, opening the spacing beyond the briefed value, but recognized the excess and closed it with a controlled power setting without prompting, with no IP input needed. Starting the timing count from the correct reference point, rather than adjusting the excess afterward, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid timing of brake release for the interval.
texts_above.3: SP released brakes at the briefed interval behind lead, timed from the correct reference point of lead's takeoff roll, so the spacing at lift-off matched the briefed value and required no power change beyond the normal takeoff setting. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed timing of brake release for the interval.
texts_above.4: SP established the briefed takeoff interval exactly, with brake release timed to the second and power applied in one continuous movement, so the rejoin geometry was set up without any corrective action. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding timing of brake release for the interval.

error_modes.label: Line up position and Line Up checks as wingman

texts.0: SP, due to a line up flown to the runway centerline instead of to the briefed wingman position, did not take the assigned line up position and did not complete the Line Up checks without omissions. The aircraft was placed on the wrong side of lead and items bearing on the takeoff configuration were left unverified when the takeoff clearance was received. IP directed the repositioning of the aircraft and confirmed the configuration before brake release.
texts.1: SP, due to workload accumulated during the formation line up, did not execute the Line Up checks without omissions. One configuration item was left unchecked and was picked up only after IP prompted for it, while the aircraft sat displaced from the briefed wingman position by an amount that had to be corrected before power application. The omissions were recovered only through IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a line up flow started later than the taxi sequence allowed, initially skipped one item of the Line Up checks and stopped short of the briefed wingman position. SP detected both on SP's own back-check, completed the item and adjusted the position before brake release, with no prompting and no IP input. The takeoff was then begun from the correct geometry.
texts.3: SP took the briefed wingman line up position relative to lead and executed the Line Up checks without omissions. Each item was verified against the actual switch position or indication, and the aircraft was ready for brake release when lead began the takeoff roll.
texts.4: SP established the wingman line up position precisely as briefed and completed the Line Up checks with a settled flow that left capacity for the takeoff clearance and the traffic picture. Everything was set and confirmed before lead started the roll, so the interval could be timed without any residual cockpit task.
texts.marginal: SP took the correct line up position and completed the Line Up checks without omissions, but the checks were run so close to lead's brake release that any interruption would have displaced an item. The standard was met on every interval takeoff of the sortie, with no item missed. SP is expected to complete the checks earlier in the line up flow so that the sequence retains margin for an interruption.

texts_at.0: SP ran the Line Up checks and took the wingman position with the sequence talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first formation line up at this stage and completing the checks without an omission prompted has not yet formed. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to complete the Line Up checks without needing an omission prompted without the reminder on the next interval takeoffs.
texts_at.1: SP recovered the omitted configuration item only through IP prompting, with the aircraft displaced from the briefed wingman position while the item was corrected before brake release. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the Line Up checks without needing an omission prompted.
texts_at.2: SP skipped one item of the Line Up checks and stopped short of the briefed wingman position, then detected both on the own back-check and completed the item and the position adjustment before brake release without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the checks and the position together rather than catching up on a back-check.
texts_at.3: SP took the briefed wingman line up position and executed the Line Up checks without omissions on three of the four takeoffs, the fourth check run close enough to brake release that an interruption would have displaced an item. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to build the same margin into that one line up that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP recovered an omitted configuration item, with the wingman position corrected before brake release from that point on. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP skipped one item of the Line Up checks and stopped short of the briefed wingman position, but detected both on the own back-check and completed the item and the position adjustment before brake release without prompting. Completing the checks and the position together, rather than catching up on a back-check, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady line up discipline as wingman.
texts_above.3: SP took the briefed wingman line up position relative to lead and executed the Line Up checks without omissions, each item verified against the actual switch position or indication, ready when lead began the takeoff roll. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate line up discipline as wingman.
texts_above.4: SP established the wingman line up position precisely as briefed and completed the Line Up checks with a settled flow that left capacity for the takeoff clearance and the traffic picture, everything set before lead started the roll. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary line up discipline as wingman.

error_modes.label: Takeoff attitude, configuration cleanup and climb profile matched to lead

texts.0: SP, due to a rotation made at a rate the pitch reference could not be tracked at while lead was kept in sight, did not bring and maintain the A/C to the proper takeoff attitude. The pitch then oscillated through the transition, the gear and flaps were retracted outside the sequence used by lead, and the airspeed deviation exceeded 10 knots against a standard that allows no low-side tolerance. IP intervened on the controls to set the attitude and to restore the climb profile.
texts.1: SP, due to pitch corrections made against the outside picture alone without reference to the attitude indication, did not maintain the proper takeoff and climbing attitude. The airspeed deviation reached the limit of the allowed tolerance and the configuration was cleaned late relative to lead, corrected only after repeated verbal direction from IP. The climb was established out of step with the leader's profile.
texts.2: SP, due to a stick input released before the takeoff attitude was fully set, allowed the pitch to settle below the proper attitude and the cleanup to begin later than planned. The resulting airspeed deviation stayed between the code 3 and code 1 limits, and SP reset the attitude, cleaned the aircraft and stabilized the climb without prompting or IP control input.
texts.3: SP brought the A/C to the proper takeoff attitude with a smooth rotation, cleaned the configuration without violating the speed limit and established the climbing attitude promptly. The climb airspeed was held inside 5 knots of standard, keeping the profile aligned with the leader's.
texts.4: SP set the takeoff attitude in one continuous input, held it with no perceptible excursion through lift-off, and retracted gear and flaps at the correct points of the profile. The climb airspeed was maintained with negligible deviation, so the geometry on lead developed exactly as briefed.
texts.marginal: SP established the takeoff and climbing attitudes and cleaned the configuration within standards, but each attitude was reached through a small overshoot followed by a correction rather than being captured directly. The airspeed excursions stayed inside tolerance and did not repeat in the same direction. SP is expected to capture the attitude on the first input, so that attention can move to lead rather than to a pitch correction.

texts_at.0: SP flew the takeoff attitude and the configuration cleanup with the attitude indication and the outside picture talked through by the IP together, because this is SP's first interval takeoff at this stage and referencing the attitude indication as well as the outside picture has not yet formed. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to reference the attitude indication as well as the outside picture without the reminder on the next interval takeoffs.
texts_at.1: SP held the airspeed deviation to about 10 knots against a standard with no low-side tolerance, at the tolerance limit, because pitch corrections were made against the outside picture alone until IP directed repeated correction. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reference the attitude indication as well as the outside picture so the deviation does not run to the edge of the tolerance.
texts_at.2: SP let the airspeed deviation reach roughly 7 knots, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the stick input was released before the takeoff attitude was fully set. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold the stick input until the attitude is fully set rather than releasing it early.
texts_at.3: SP held the climb airspeed inside 5 knots of standard on three of the four departures, keeping the profile aligned with lead's, the fourth needing a small correction after an attitude reached through a small overshoot. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to capture that one attitude on the first input as cleanly as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP referenced the attitude indication alongside the outside picture, holding the airspeed deviation to about 10 knots against a standard with no low-side tolerance, at the tolerance limit. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP let the pitch settle below the proper attitude and the cleanup begin a little late but reset the attitude, cleaned the aircraft and stabilized the climb without prompting or IP control input, holding the airspeed deviation to about 7 knots. Holding the stick input until the attitude is fully set, rather than releasing it early, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable attitude and configuration matching to lead.
texts_above.3: SP brought the aircraft to the proper takeoff attitude with a smooth rotation, cleaned the configuration without violating the speed limit and established the climbing attitude promptly, holding the climb airspeed inside 5 knots of standard. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good attitude and configuration matching to lead.
texts_above.4: SP set the takeoff attitude in one continuous input, held it with no perceptible excursion through lift-off, and retracted gear and flaps at the correct points so the geometry on lead developed exactly as briefed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior attitude and configuration matching to lead.

error_modes.label: Visual contact with lead and avoidance of wake and jet wash

texts.0: SP, due to situational awareness limited to the cockpit instruments during the acceleration, lost visual contact with lead and did not stay clear of the wake behind him. The aircraft was flown into the disturbed air on lead's extended track and was displaced in roll while still low and accelerating, with no lateral offset established. IP took the controls to move the aircraft out of the wake and to re-establish visual contact with lead.
texts.1: SP, due to degraded situational awareness of lead's position after lift-off, did not establish the briefed lateral offset from lead's track. The aircraft remained on the leader's extended centerline at spacing near the minimum of the acceptable band, and SP displaced only after IP called the wake hazard. Visual contact was regained late and through IP direction rather than by SP's own lookout.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the airspeed indication during the initial climb, allowed the aircraft to drift back toward lead's track after lift-off. The offset reduced but stayed inside the acceptable band, and SP recognized the geometry, re-established the briefed displacement and kept lead in sight throughout, without prompting or IP input.
texts.3: SP maintained visual contact with lead from brake release through the departure and held the briefed lateral offset from the leader's track. The aircraft stayed clear of the wake at all times, with the offset set early rather than corrected later.
texts.4: SP kept lead in sight continuously and established the lateral offset as the aircraft became airborne, with the wake region avoided by a comfortable margin throughout the climb. The lookout was maintained without any loss of accuracy on the takeoff parameters.
texts.marginal: SP kept lead in sight and remained clear of the wake, but the lateral offset was set at the minimum acceptable value and only after the gear was up. The standard was met and no wake encounter occurred on any takeoff of the sortie. SP is expected to establish the offset as the aircraft lifts off, so that the clearance from the wake does not depend on lead's exact track.

texts_at.0: SP established the lateral offset from lead's wake with the offset point talked through by the IP as the aircraft became airborne, because this is SP's first interval takeoff at this stage and establishing the briefed lateral offset without a prompt has not yet formed. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to establish the briefed lateral offset without needing visual contact regained by direction without the reminder on the next interval takeoffs.
texts_at.1: SP regained visual contact with lead only through IP direction, having remained on lead's extended centerline at spacing near the minimum of the acceptable band after lift-off. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to establish the briefed lateral offset without needing visual contact regained by direction.
texts_at.2: SP let the aircraft drift back toward lead's track after lift-off because attention was held on the airspeed indication, then recognized the geometry and re-established the briefed displacement without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to divide attention between the airspeed and the offset from lead rather than losing the offset while checking the airspeed.
texts_at.3: SP maintained visual contact with lead and held the briefed lateral offset on three of the four departures, the fourth needing a small correction after the offset was recognized a beat late. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold that same offset on every departure that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP regained visual contact with lead, having remained near the minimum spacing on lead's extended centerline before the offset was established. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP let the aircraft drift back toward lead's track after lift-off because attention was held on the airspeed indication, but recognized the geometry and re-established the briefed displacement without prompting, keeping lead in sight throughout. Dividing attention between the airspeed and the offset from lead, rather than losing the offset while checking the airspeed, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured visual contact and wake avoidance.
texts_above.3: SP maintained visual contact with lead from brake release through the departure and held the briefed lateral offset from the leader's track, with the offset set early rather than corrected later and clear of the wake at all times. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise visual contact and wake avoidance.
texts_above.4: SP kept lead in sight continuously and established the lateral offset as the aircraft became airborne, with the wake region avoided by a comfortable margin throughout the climb and no loss of accuracy on the takeoff parameters. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate visual contact and wake avoidance.

error_modes.label: Closure control and power management during the post-takeoff rejoin

texts.0: SP, due to a perceptual error in judging closure and lateral separation on lead, did not control the overtake during the post-takeoff rejoin. The aircraft closed with excess airspeed well above the briefed rejoin differential and arrived inside the briefed minimum separation with the geometry still developing. IP took the controls to reduce power and to stop the overtake before the aircraft passed the leader's line.
texts.1: SP, due to a perceptual error in judging closure rate against lead, did not reduce power at the point the rejoin required. The overtake persisted with the airspeed differential at the limit of the acceptable band, and SP stabilized the closure only after IP called for a power reduction. The rejoin was completed late and with the position corrected under direction.
texts.2: SP, due to a decision to hold rejoin power slightly longer than the closure supported, allowed the overtake on lead to build past the briefed differential. The excess remained between the code 3 and code 1 limits, and SP recognized the closure against the leader's wingspan and reduced power to stabilize the rejoin without prompting or IP input.
texts.3: SP controlled the closure on lead throughout the rejoin, holding the briefed airspeed differential and reducing power at the point that produced a stabilized arrival. The aircraft stopped in the briefed position with no overshoot and no corrective input required.
texts.4: SP managed the rejoin with power and geometry adjusted continuously to the observed closure, arriving in the briefed position with a differential that decayed exactly to zero. There was no overshoot, no oscillation on the position and no need to reset the geometry.
texts.marginal: SP controlled the closure within standards but arrived at the rejoin position with the airspeed differential still at the high end of the acceptable band, requiring a firm power reduction at the end. No overshoot occurred and the position was stabilized on each rejoin of the sortie. SP is expected to start the power reduction earlier, so that the closure is bled off progressively rather than in one late input.

texts_at.0: SP controlled the closure on lead during the post-takeoff rejoin with the point for reducing power talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first post-takeoff rejoin at this stage and reducing power at the point the rejoin requires it has not yet formed. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to reduce power at the point the rejoin requires it without the reminder on the next rejoins.
texts_at.1: SP stabilized the closure on lead only after IP called for a power reduction, with the airspeed differential at the limit of the acceptable band while the rejoin was completed under direction. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce power at the point the rejoin requires it without needing the reduction called.
texts_at.2: SP allowed the overtake on lead to build past the briefed differential after holding rejoin power slightly longer than the closure supported, then recognized the closure against the leader's wingspan and reduced power to stabilize the rejoin without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to judge the closure against the leader's wingspan earlier rather than after the differential has already built.
texts_at.3: SP controlled the closure on lead and held the briefed airspeed differential on three of the four rejoins, reducing power at the point that produced a stabilized arrival, the fourth needing a firmer reduction after closure judged a beat late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to judge that one closure with the same timing the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP stabilized the closure on lead, with the airspeed differential at the limit of the acceptable band before power was reduced. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP allowed the overtake on lead to build past the briefed differential after holding rejoin power slightly longer than the closure supported, but recognized the closure against the leader's wingspan and reduced power to stabilize the rejoin without prompting. Judging the closure against the leader's wingspan earlier, rather than after the differential has built, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent closure control on the post-takeoff rejoin.
texts_above.3: SP controlled the closure on lead throughout the rejoin, holding the briefed airspeed differential and reducing power at the point that produced a stabilized arrival with no overshoot and no corrective input required. texts.0: SP, due to a PCL advance made while attention stayed on lead's position down the runway, did not begin the takeoff roll in MAX power as the interval takeoff requires. The aircraft accelerated with less than takeoff power, the spacing behind lead opened far beyond the geometry produced by the 10 second interval, and the late shove to MAX then drove the airspeed more than 10 knots past the standard while the aircraft was cleaning up. Power was retarded and braking applied with the other aircraft already decelerating ahead, adding a second aircraft to the high speed abort situation, and the deceleration was made with the track more than 10 feet off the assigned line. IP took the controls to stop the abort and to keep the aircraft on its side of the runway.

The power reduction and the initial braking took the track to about 10 feet from the assigned line, at the limit of the allowed deviation, and SP resumed the takeoff only after IP stated that no sympathetic abort was required. The recovery of takeoff power was late and the sequence was completed under direction.
texts.2: SP, due to a momentary reaction to lead's abort call, relaxed the PCL after brake release before checking SP's own aircraft state. The speed loss was small and the track displaced roughly 8 feet from the assigned line, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, and SP recognized that no sympathetic abort applied and restored MAX power on SP's own initiative with runway remaining.
texts.3: SP kept MAX power set after brake release when lead aborted, applying the rule that there are normally no sympathetic aborts once the roll has begun, and continued the takeoff on his own side of the runway. Directional control was maintained inside 5 feet of the assigned line and separation from the aborting aircraft was preserved throughout.
texts.4: SP assessed his own aircraft and position without any change to the takeoff power when the abort was called ahead, and flew a normal takeoff on the assigned side of the runway. There was no hesitation on the PCL, no speed loss and no perceptible deviation from the assigned line, so no additional aircraft was introduced into the high speed abort situation.
texts.marginal: SP continued the takeoff correctly after lead's abort but with a visible hesitation on the PCL before the decision was consolidated. Speed and track stayed inside standards and the takeoff was completed without prompting. SP is expected to check his own aircraft state first and to hold takeoff power, so that the reaction to the call does not become a sympathetic abort.

texts.marginal: SP took the correct action for his speed but only after visibly working through the decision during the roll, consuming runway that a prepared decision would have preserved. The aircraft stayed inside standards and stopped safely on its own side of the runway. SP is expected to have the abort criteria set before brake release, so the action follows the recognition without an intermediate decision phase.

texts_at.0: SP compared own speed with abort speed when lead aborted with the decision framework talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first abort-speed decision at this stage and comparing own speed with abort speed at the point the situation requires it has not yet formed. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to compare own speed with abort speed at the point the situation requires it without the reminder on the next interval takeoffs.
texts_at.1: SP had the correct action stated by IP before it was taken, with the track about 10 feet from the assigned line, at the tolerance limit, because the decision was left unresolved while own speed was not checked against abort speed promptly. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to compare own speed with abort speed at the point the situation requires it, without needing the action stated.
texts_at.2: SP took the required action later than the situation allowed because of a short delay in checking the airspeed indication against abort speed, with the track displacing roughly 8 feet during the initial deceleration, then completed the abort on the own initiative with runway remaining. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check the airspeed indication against abort speed as soon as the situation requires it rather than after a short delay.
texts_at.3: SP applied the interval takeoff rules correctly, checking own speed against abort speed and holding the track inside 5 feet on three of the four occasions, the fourth check made a beat later than ideal. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make that one check as promptly as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP took the correct action once it was stated by the IP, holding the track to about 10 feet from the assigned line, at the tolerance limit. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP took the required action later than the situation allowed because of a short delay in checking the airspeed indication against abort speed, but completed the abort on the own initiative with runway remaining, holding the track to about 8 feet from the assigned line. Checking the airspeed indication against abort speed as soon as the situation requires it, rather than after a short delay, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured abort or continue decision discipline.
texts_above.3: SP applied the interval takeoff rules correctly, checking own speed against abort speed and executing the abort as required when rolling below it, with the aircraft kept inside 5 feet of the assigned line and runway remaining at the stop. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise abort or continue decision discipline.
texts_above.4: SP had the decision framework set before brake release and acted on it immediately, with negligible deviation from the assigned line and ample runway remaining regardless of the speed at which the abort was called. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate abort or continue decision discipline.

error_modes.label: Aircraft control given up to make a radio call during a takeoff abnormality
error_modes.source: technique:9.42 FORMATION TAKEOFF ABNORMALITIES AND ABORTS

texts.0: SP, due to priority given to transmitting before flying, sacrificed aircraft control to make a radio call while the abnormality was still developing on the runway. Directional inputs stopped while the transmission was composed, the aircraft diverged more than 10 feet from the assigned line and the deceleration was flown without a stable track. IP took the controls to re establish directional control and completed the radio call afterwards.
texts.1: SP, due to an attempt to pass the call at the same moment as the initial control inputs, allowed the track to deteriorate while transmitting. The displacement reached about 10 feet from the assigned line, at the limit of the allowed deviation, and SP returned to the controls only after IP called for aircraft control first. The transmission was made correctly but at the cost of the track.
texts.2: SP, due to a radio call made slightly earlier than the aircraft state allowed, let the directional corrections lapse for a short period during the roll. The track drifted roughly 8 feet from the assigned line, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, and SP recognized the lapse, resumed the rudder corrections and re centered the aircraft without prompting.
texts.3: SP flew the aircraft first and made the radio call as soon as practical, without sacrificing aircraft control to transmit. Directional control was continuous through the abnormality and the track was held inside 5 feet of the assigned line.
texts.4: SP maintained full directional control throughout, transmitted only when the aircraft state permitted and kept the call short and standard. The track showed no perceptible change while the call was being made and separation from the other aircraft was preserved at all times.
texts.marginal: SP kept aircraft control adequate while transmitting, but the call was made at the busiest point of the roll and small track corrections had to follow it. Deviations remained inside standards and no IP action was needed. SP is expected to delay the transmission until as soon as practical, so that aircraft control is never traded for a radio call.

texts_at.0: SP handled the takeoff abnormality with the priority of aircraft control over the radio call talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first takeoff abnormality at this stage and keeping the directional inputs running through the transmission has not yet formed. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to keep the directional inputs running through the transmission without the reminder on the next interval takeoffs.
texts_at.1: SP returned to the controls only after IP called for aircraft control first, with the track about 10 feet from the assigned line, at the tolerance limit, because directional inputs stopped while the radio transmission was composed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the directional inputs running through the transmission rather than needing aircraft control called for first.
texts_at.2: SP let the directional corrections lapse for a short period because the radio call was made slightly earlier than the aircraft state allowed, with the track drifting roughly 8 feet from the assigned line, then resumed the rudder corrections and re-centered the aircraft without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to judge the aircraft state before making the call rather than resuming the corrections after a lapse.
texts_at.3: SP flew the aircraft first and made the radio call as soon as practical on three of the four occasions, holding the track inside 5 feet, the fourth call made a moment before the aircraft state fully allowed it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to judge that one call with the same timing the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP returned to aircraft control once it was called for ahead of the radio call, holding the track to about 10 feet from the assigned line, at the tolerance limit. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP let the directional corrections lapse for a short period because the radio call was made slightly earlier than the aircraft state allowed, but resumed the rudder corrections and re-centered the aircraft without prompting, holding the track to about 8 feet from the assigned line. Judging the aircraft state before making the call, rather than resuming the corrections after a lapse, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent aircraft control priority during a radio call.
texts_above.3: SP flew the aircraft first and made the radio call as soon as practical, without sacrificing aircraft control to transmit, holding directional control continuous through the abnormality with the track inside 5 feet of the assigned line. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed aircraft control priority during a radio call.
texts_above.4: SP maintained full directional control throughout, transmitting only when the aircraft state permitted and keeping the call short and standard, with no perceptible change in the track while the call was being made. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding aircraft control priority during a radio call.

error_modes.label: Maintaining the respective side of the runway during an abort or a separate takeoff
error_modes.source: technique:9.42 FORMATION TAKEOFF ABNORMALITIES AND ABORTS

texts.0: SP, due to a track flown to the runway centerline instead of to the respective side after the abnormality, did not ensure separation from the other aircraft. The aircraft crossed into the half of the runway occupied by lead by more than 10 feet while both aircraft were still decelerating or accelerating, so the only remaining separation was longitudinal. IP took the controls to move the aircraft back to its assigned side of the runway.
texts.1: SP, due to directional corrections referenced to the centerline rather than to the assigned side, allowed the aircraft to converge with the other aircraft's half of the runway. The displacement from the assigned line reached about 10 feet, at the limit of the allowed deviation, and SP re established the correct side only after IP called for separation. The separate takeoff was then completed under direction.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow reaction to the drift produced by the power change, moved off the assigned side of the runway by roughly 8 feet after passing the other aircraft. The deviation stayed between the code 3 and code 1 limits and SP recognized it against the runway markings and returned to the assigned side without prompting or IP input.
texts.3: SP maintained the respective side of the runway throughout the abnormality, selecting MAX power for the separate takeoff and holding the assigned line inside 5 feet. Lateral separation from the other aircraft was preserved from the first indication of the problem to lift off, and lead's directions were followed as given.
texts.4: SP held the aircraft exactly on its assigned side of the runway from the first indication of the abnormality through the separate takeoff, with the power change producing no perceptible drift. Lateral separation was never reduced and the aircraft was positioned to follow lead's directions at any moment.
texts.marginal: SP stayed on the respective side of the runway but tracked close to the centerline for much of the separate takeoff, so the lateral separation was at the lower end of the acceptable band. No deviation exceeded standards and no correction was called for. SP is expected to keep the aircraft well within its own half, so that the separation from the other aircraft does not depend on small track errors.

texts_at.0: SP held the respective side of the runway during the abnormality with the assigned side reference talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first takeoff abnormality at this stage and referencing the assigned side of the runway directly has not yet formed. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to reference the assigned side of the runway directly rather than the centerline without the reminder on the next interval takeoffs.
texts_at.1: SP re-established the correct side of the runway only after IP called for separation, with the displacement about 10 feet from the assigned line, at the tolerance limit, because the directional corrections were referenced to the centerline rather than to the assigned side. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reference the assigned side of the runway directly rather than the centerline, so separation does not need to be called.
texts_at.2: SP moved off the assigned side of the runway by roughly 8 feet after passing the other aircraft, because the reaction to the drift produced by the power change was slow, then recognized it against the runway markings and returned to the own side without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to react to the drift produced by the power change as promptly as the correction that followed it.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the respective side of the runway inside 5 feet on three of the four occasions during the abnormality, the fourth needing a small correction after a reaction to the drift that came a beat late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold that same margin on every occasion that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP re-established the correct side of the runway once separation was called for, holding the displacement to about 10 feet from the assigned line, at the tolerance limit. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP moved off the assigned side of the runway by roughly 8 feet after passing the other aircraft, because the reaction to the drift produced by the power change was slow, but recognized it against the runway markings and returned to the own side without prompting or IP input. Reacting to the drift produced by the power change as promptly as the correction that followed, rather than after the drift builds, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound runway side discipline during an abnormality.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the respective side of the runway throughout the abnormality, selecting MAX power for the separate takeoff and holding the assigned line inside 5 feet, with lateral separation from the other aircraft preserved from the first indication of the problem. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed runway side discipline during an abnormality.
texts_above.4: SP held the aircraft exactly on the assigned side of the runway from the first indication of the abnormality through the separate takeoff, with the power change producing no perceptible drift and lateral separation never reduced. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional runway side discipline during an abnormality.
